t.1.208.1: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the bull among the Bharatas went to the most holy tīrthas on the southern ocean, which were graced by ascetics.
t.1.208.2: But the ascetics there avoided five sacred fords, which had formerly been frequented by men of austerity.
t.1.208.3: The Agastya Tīrtha, the Saubhadra, and the most purifying Pauloma, the clear Kāraṃdhama, which yields the fruit of a horse sacrifice, and the great tīrtha of Bhāradvāja, which destroys sin.
t.1.208.4: Then the Pāṇḍava, noticing that those tīrthas were deserted, and seeing that they were shunned by the sages whose minds were set on dharma,
t.1.208.5: Then the delight of the Kurus, with joined palms, asked the ascetics: "For what reason are these sacred fords avoided by the expounders of the Veda?"
t.1.208.6: Five crocodiles dwell in these, and they carry off ascetics rich in austerity; therefore these tīrthas are avoided, O joy of the Kurus.
t.1.208.7: Having heard them, the mighty-armed one, best of men, though restrained by the ascetics rich in austerity, went to see those sacred fords.
t.1.208.8: Then, reaching Saubhadra, the supreme tīrtha of the great seer, the hero, scorcher of foes, plunged in swiftly and bathed.
t.1.208.9: Then a great crocodile, a creature moving beneath the water, seized in the water that tiger among men, Dhanaṃjaya, the son of Kuntī.
t.1.208.10: Seizing that thrashing water-creature, the mighty-armed son of Kuntī, best of the strong, rose up by his strength.
t.1.208.11: But as soon as that crocodile was dragged out by the glorious Arjuna, it became a lovely woman adorned with every ornament, blazing with splendor, O king, of divine form and enchanting to the heart.
t.1.208.12: Seeing that great marvel, Dhanaṃjaya, the son of Kuntī, supremely delighted, spoke these words to that woman.
t.1.208.13: Who are you, lovely one, and from where have you come, you who move in the water? And for what reason did you commit this great sin in the past?
t.1.208.14: I am an Apsaras, O mighty-armed one, who roams the forests of the gods, ever beloved of the Lord of Wealth; my name is Vargā, O mighty one.
t.1.208.15: I had four other friends, all lovely and able to go wherever they wished; together with them I set out for the dwelling of the guardian of the world.
t.1.208.17: By his austerity, O king, that forest was enveloped in splendor; like the sun, he lit up that entire region.
t.1.208.16: Then all of us saw a brahmin of rigorous vows, handsome, reciting the Veda, alone and dwelling in solitude.
t.1.208.18: Having seen his austerity of such a kind and his form, wondrous to behold, we descended to that place with the desire to create an obstacle to his austerity.
t.1.208.19: I and Saurabheyī, Samīcī, Budbudā and Latā all approached that brahmin at the same time, O Bhārata.
t.1.208.20: Singing, laughing and trying to tempt that twice-born, we gave him no peace; yet in no way, O hero, did he set his mind upon us. That greatly radiant one did not waver, but remained steadfast in his spotless austerity.
t.1.208.21: But that brāhmaṇa, enraged, cursed us, O bull among kṣatriyas: “Having become crocodiles, you shall roam in the water for a hundred years.”
